title: Section 91 — Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

content.overview: BNS s. 91 — Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth. BNS restatement of IPC 315. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 315. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 91 is the rule on “Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth”. The section provides that whoever before the birth of any child does any act with the intention of thereby preventing that child from being born alive or causing it to die after its birth, and does by such act prevent that child from being born alive, or causes it to die after its birth, shall, if such act be not caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 91 exists so that “Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth” has a closed legal test in Chapter V — Of Offences Against Woman and Child. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Sexual offences, assault, marriage, miscarriage, and offences against the child — placed first among the offence chapters.

enhancement.definition: BNS s. 91 penalizes whoever, before the birth of any child, does any act with the intention of thereby preventing that child from being born alive or causing it to die after its birth, and does by such act prevent that child from being born alive, or causes it to die after its birth, punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both, unless caused in good faith for saving the life of the mother.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes intentional destruction of fetal life immediately prior to or during delivery, bridging the legal gap between miscarriage and homicide of a living human being.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 91 (corresponding to IPC s. 315).
Timing: Act done before the birth of any child.
Intent: Intention to prevent the child from being born alive, or causing it to die after birth.
Result: Successfully prevents live birth or causes death after birth.
Exception: Act done in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother.
Punishment: Imprisonment of either description extending up to ten years, or fine, or both.
essentialIngredients: An act was done before the birth of the child.
The act was done with the specific intention of preventing the child from being born alive, or causing it to die after its birth.
The act succeeded in preventing the child from being born alive, or caused it to die after birth.
The act was NOT caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 91 occupies a unique place in penal law, commonly described as the offence of infanticide or feticide at the threshold of birth. In criminal law, causing the death of a fetus in the womb is not culpable homicide (as the child is not yet a 'person' in being under homicide law), while killing a fully born child is murder. Section 91 bridges this gap by criminalizing acts done before birth designed to ensure the child does not emerge alive or perishes immediately after birth. The actus reus must occur before delivery, but the fatal effect may manifest either in utero (stillbirth) or after delivery (death shortly following birth). A strict exception exists where medical practitioners perform procedures in good faith to save the mother's life during obstructed or fatal labor.
examples: Teaching example (Preventing live birth during delivery): An unqualified attendant deliberately crushes the skull of an infant during labor or administers a lethal substance to ensure the child is born dead. This constitutes an offence under s. 91.

Teaching example (Emergency craniotomy to save mother): A qualified obstetrician performs a destructive procedure on a dead or impacted fetus during obstructed labor solely to save the mother from fatal uterine rupture. The doctor is protected by the good-faith life-saving exception.
distinctions: Section 91 vs Miscarriage (s. 88): Miscarriage involves premature expulsion of the fetus at earlier gestational stages; Section 91 typically applies to advanced or full-term pregnancies where the intent is to prevent a viable child from being born alive.
Section 91 vs Murder (s. 103): Murder requires the victim to be a living human being who has completely emerged from the mother's body; Section 91 applies where the act was committed before birth.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who assaulted a full-term pregnant woman on her abdomen with the explicit intent that the child not be born alive, resulting in intra-uterine fetal death, is liable under s. 91.
Rule: Doing an act before birth with intent to prevent live birth which succeeds in causing stillbirth satisfies BNS s. 91.
Application: The physical blow was directed at the abdomen of a full-term fetus with specific intent to kill the child before birth.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 91.
